cards.front: What are computational thinking's three main principles?
cards.answer: Abstraction / Decomposition / Algorithmic thinking

cards.front: Why is Harry Beck's Underground map still useful even though it is geographically 'wrong'?
cards.answer: It keeps only the station order, line and connections that passengers need, which is more useful than true geography.

cards.front: Why does naming a variable something sensible like score or playerName count as abstraction?
cards.answer: It lets you think about what the data means while hiding the binary and memory detail underneath.

cards.front: What four tools does the lesson give for designing an algorithm?
cards.answer: Working out inputs and outputs / Drawing structure diagrams / Writing pseudocode / Drawing a flowchart

cards.front: What are the six standard flowchart symbols?
cards.answer: Terminal / Process / Input/output / Decision / Sub program / Flow line

cards.front: Why do programmers often prefer pseudocode for longer algorithm designs?
cards.answer: It is quick to write and translates easily into real code in any programming language.

cards.front: Why are flowcharts especially useful for explaining an algorithm to someone else?
cards.answer: They are more visual and make branching and loops easy to see at a glance.

cards.front: Why does a linear search work on a list in any order?
cards.answer: It never assumes anything about the order of the data, so it works on a list in any order.

cards.front: Why can a binary search rule out large parts of a sorted list in one comparison?
cards.answer: Because the list is already in order, everything on the wrong side of the middle item is guaranteed not to match.

cards.front: Which three sorting algorithms does the lesson cover?
cards.answer: Bubble sort / Insertion sort / Merge sort

cards.front: Why does insertion sort often need to move each new item only a short distance?
cards.answer: Because it shifts items along to make room rather than swapping repeatedly across the whole list.

cards.front: Why does merge sort cope much better than bubble sort with large lists?
cards.answer: The amount of work merge sort does grows much more gently as the list gets longer than bubble sort's does.

cards.front: What are the three constructs that control the flow of any program?
cards.answer: Sequence / Selection / Iteration

cards.front: What are the six comparison operators listed in the lesson?
cards.answer: Equal to (==) / Not equal to (!=) / Less than (<) / Less than or equal to (<=) / Greater than (>) / Greater than or equal to (>=)

cards.front: Why does x = x + 1 make sense in programming but not in maths?
cards.answer: In programming the equals sign is an instruction to store a value, not a question about whether two things are equal.

cards.front: Why do you need AND rather than OR when checking a registrant is aged 13 or over and has agreed to the terms?
cards.answer: Because AND requires both conditions to be true, while OR would let someone register with just one of them met.

cards.front: What are the five basic data types covered in the lesson?
cards.answer: Integer / Real (float) / Boolean / Character / String

cards.front: What three things does choosing the right data type affect, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Which operations are allowed / How much memory is used / Catching invalid data early

cards.front: Why is a 2D array useful for representing a game board?
cards.answer: It adds a second index so it behaves like a grid of rows and columns, matching the board's layout.

cards.front: Why are arrays and loops so often used together?
cards.answer: A single loop can visit each index in turn, so the same few lines work whether there are 30 items or 3000.

cards.front: What are the four basic file operations given in the lesson?
cards.answer: Open a file / Read from it / Write to it / Close it

cards.front: Why does a function normally need its return value stored in a variable?
cards.answer: Because a function produces a result, you need to store what it returns in order to use it later.

cards.front: Why do global variables make it harder to track down bugs?
cards.answer: If many sub programs can all change the same global value, tracking down which one caused a bug becomes much harder.

cards.front: What are the five common validation checks listed in the lesson?
cards.answer: Presence / Range / Type / Length / Format

cards.front: What four techniques improve maintainability, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Using sub programs to avoid repeated code / Following clear naming conventions / Indenting code to show structure / Adding comments to explain the code
items: Using sub programs to avoid repeated code
Adding comments to explain the code

cards.front: Why does every extra character in a password matter so much for security?
cards.answer: Each extra character multiplies the number of possible combinations an attacker would have to try, making guessing impractical.

cards.front: Why is tangled, poorly organised code more likely to gain new bugs when someone edits it?
cards.answer: Code that is tidy and clearly explained can be changed safely, but a tangled mess is where new mistakes creep in.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the systematic debugging routine, in order?
cards.answer: Read the error message carefully / Narrow down which module has the fault / Trace the suspect section by hand / Change one thing at a time and re-test
items: Narrow down which module has the fault
Trace the suspect section by hand
Change one thing at a time and re-test

cards.front: Why does iterative testing save time compared with testing only at the very end?
cards.answer: Because each module is already known to work, so any new bug is almost certainly in the code just added.

cards.front: Why should you change only one thing at a time when debugging?
cards.answer: So you always know exactly which fix actually worked, since changing lots of things at once tends to create new bugs.

cards.front: What are the four different ways of describing the same logic system, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: A written description in plain English / A Boolean expression / A logic diagram of gates / A truth table
items: A written description in plain English

cards.front: Why can an AND gate be pictured as two switches wired in series?
cards.answer: The current can only flow through both switches, and so give an output, when both are closed at the same time.

cards.front: Why are logic gates found inside the arithmetic logic unit (ALU) of a processor?
cards.answer: Because the ALU is the part of the processor that carries out calculations and logical comparisons, built from combinations of gates.

cards.front: What four kinds of tool does an IDE usually provide?
cards.answer: Editor / Error diagnostics / Run-time environment / Translator

cards.front: Why does giving someone a compiled executable protect your source code?
cards.answer: Because the executable runs on its own without needing the original source code to be shared.

cards.front: What are the six comparison operators SQL WHERE conditions can use?
cards.answer: Equal to (=) / Not equal to (<>) / Less than (<) / Greater than (>) / Less than or equal to (<=) / Greater than or equal to (>=)

cards.front: Why does forgetting the quotes around a text value in a WHERE condition cause an error?
cards.answer: Without quotes, the database reads the word as the name of a field rather than as a piece of text to match.

cards.front: Why does a WHERE clause using OR always return at least as many records as the same clause using AND?
cards.answer: OR keeps a record when at least one condition is true, a looser test than AND needing both true.

cards.front: Why is it easy to confuse a string's length with its last valid index?
cards.answer: Length counts characters starting at one, but indexes start at zero, so the last index is always length minus one.

cards.front: Why do ASC and CHR let you build a simple substitution cipher?
cards.answer: Because the codes for the letters run in order, so arithmetic on a code shifts a letter along the alphabet.

cards.front: What are the three stages of the fetch-execute cycle, in order?
cards.answer: Fetch the next instruction / Decode it / Execute it

cards.front: What are the four main parts of the CPU described in the lesson?
cards.answer: Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) / Control Unit (CU) / Cache / Registers

cards.front: Why does the CPU keep a cache instead of fetching everything from main memory?
cards.answer: Main memory is slower, so a small block of very fast memory nearby lets the CPU grab frequently used data almost instantly.

cards.front: What three characteristics have the biggest effect on CPU performance?
cards.answer: Clock speed / Cache size / Number of cores

cards.front: What are the three levels of CPU cache, from fastest to slowest?
cards.answer: L1 cache / L2 cache / L3 cache

cards.front: Why might a CPU with a very high clock speed but a tiny cache still perform poorly?
cards.answer: It may keep stalling while it waits for data to arrive from the slower RAM.

cards.front: Why do the extra heat and power draw from a high clock speed and many cores matter especially for laptops and phones?
cards.answer: Both draw more power and produce more heat, and laptops and phones have limited battery life and cooling.

cards.front: What five typical characteristics do embedded systems share, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Dedicated to one function / Small / Low-power / Low-cost / Reliable

cards.front: Why is limited flexibility the main trade-off of choosing an embedded system over a full computer?
cards.answer: Its hardware and firmware are built for one job and cannot easily be given new tasks or upgraded.

cards.front: What three features does the lesson use to compare RAM and ROM?
cards.answer: Whether it is volatile / Whether it can be written to / What it stores
items: Whether it can be written to

cards.front: Why is RAM compared to the top of a desk rather than a filing cabinet?
cards.answer: Like a desk top, RAM holds what you are using right now so you can reach it quickly, unlike a filing cabinet you must fetch from.

cards.front: What are the three main families of secondary storage?
cards.answer: Magnetic storage / Optical storage / Solid-state storage

cards.front: What six characteristics are used to compare types of secondary storage?
cards.answer: Capacity / Speed / Portability / Durability / Reliability / Cost

cards.front: Why is a solid-state drive usually the best fit for an everyday laptop despite its higher cost?
cards.answer: Speed and durability matter more for a laptop than the extra cost, and an SSD is fast, robust, silent and saves battery.

cards.front: Why is an optical disc still a good choice for handing out a film to many people despite its small capacity?
cards.answer: It is cheap to produce in bulk and easy to carry, and the small capacity is enough for the files.

cards.front: What are the four simple rules for adding binary digits?
Why is hexadecimal a popular shorthand for binary among programmers?
cards.answer: It is compact and lines up neatly with binary, since one hex digit represents exactly one nibble of 4 bits.

cards.front: Why was Unicode created even though ASCII already existed?
cards.answer: ASCII's 128 characters were not nearly enough for every writing system, so Unicode uses more bits to represent over a million characters.

cards.front: Why does 24-bit 'true colour' produce smooth, realistic images?
cards.answer: It stores over 16 million shades, more than the human eye can easily tell apart.

cards.front: Why does a low-resolution image look blocky when stretched across a large screen?
cards.answer: Because each pixel is enlarged until you can see the individual squares.

cards.front: Why can lossless compression usually not shrink a file as much as lossy compression can?
cards.answer: Because it is only allowed to reorganise data, never to remove it.

cards.front: Why does run-length encoding work poorly on a detailed photograph?
cards.answer: Colours rarely repeat in a detailed photo, so there are few long runs of the same value to shrink.

cards.front: What five pieces of hardware build a LAN, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Network Interface Controller (NIC) / Switch / Router / Wireless access point / Transmission media

cards.front: Why is a peer-to-peer network cheaper to set up than a client-server network but harder to secure?
cards.answer: There is no expensive central server to buy, but with no central point, backups and security are harder to manage.

cards.front: Why is a wired connection generally considered more secure than a wireless one?
cards.answer: An intruder needs physical access to the cable, whereas a wireless signal can be intercepted without it.

cards.front: What are the six common forms of network attack listed in the lesson?
cards.answer: Malware / Social engineering (e.g. phishing) / Brute-force attacks / Denial of service attacks / Data interception and theft / SQL injection

cards.front: What six prevention methods, used together, defend a network once weaknesses are found?
cards.answer: Anti-malware software / Firewalls / User access levels / Strong passwords / Encryption / Physical security

cards.front: Why do organisations layer several different security methods together rather than relying on just one?
cards.answer: If one layer fails to stop an attack, the others still stand and can catch or limit the damage.

cards.front: Why can a denial of service attack cost a business money even though no data is stolen?
cards.answer: It makes a website or service unavailable to genuine users, which damages the business's reputation and costs money.

cards.front: What are the five main jobs of an operating system?
cards.answer: Providing a user interface / Managing memory and multitasking / Managing peripherals through drivers / Managing users and access rights / Managing files

cards.front: Why might the operating system move a program's data aside even though the program is still open?
cards.answer: It frees memory for the other programs that need their turn to run at that instant.

cards.front: Why is compression especially useful for photos, music and email attachments?
cards.answer: Smaller files take up less storage space and can be sent across a network more quickly.

cards.front: What five kinds of impact does the lesson sort technology's effects into?
cards.answer: Ethical / Legal / Cultural / Environmental / Privacy

cards.front: What three main ways does digital technology harm the environment, according to the lesson?
cards.answer: Mining raw materials for devices / Electricity used by devices and data centres / E-waste from discarded equipment
items: Electricity used by devices and data centres

cards.front: Why might a school with little money but skilled staff choose open source software?
cards.answer: It saves on licence fees and lets staff customise the software to suit their lessons.

cards.front: Why can being on the wrong side of the digital divide cost someone access to jobs and education?
cards.answer: Jobs, education and services are increasingly online only, so poor access to technology shuts people out of them.
